Explain photosynthesis, respiration, and translocation in higher plants.
Explain the standard plant propagation methods.

Distinguish between soil horizons.
Interpret and explain the relationship between soil properties and other ecosystem functions, such as plant growth, moisture storage, biogeochemical cycling.

Interpret and explain the relationship between soil properties and environmental hazards.

Explain the importance of soil organisms.
Describe the process and time required for soil formation.

Recognize the theoretical approaches to human culture.
Explain the various methods used in anthropological fieldwork.
Employ the relativist perspective while discussing cultural variation.

Explain the interconnections of the economic, political and sociocultural forces of globalization among diverse cultural groups.

rows.title: Magic, Witchcraft, and Religion

Compare and contrast systems of magic, witchcraft, and religion from the past and the present and from societies around the world.

Apply anthropological research methods and theoretical approaches to the analysis of religious beliefs and practices.
Analyze the relationship between religious beliefs and practices and their social, economic, and political contexts.

Analyze and evaluate the evidence of our common human ancestry.
Compare and contrast the cultural heritages of ancient civilizations.
Explain how archaeologists find, excavate, date and analyze artifacts, and archaeological sites.

Identify and critically discriminate between good and bad evidence for human prehistory and early history.

rows.title: Physical Anthropology

outcomes: Learning Outcomes
Describe the scientific method (hypothetico-deductive reasoning) related to issues of human evolution.
Describe principles of Darwinian evolution and genetics as they apply to human ancestry.

Evaluate how the forces of evolution produce genetic and phenotypic change over time.
Recognize the major groups of hominin fossils and describe alternate phylogenies for human evolution.
Summarize methods used in interpreting the fossil record, including dating techniques.

rows.title: Physical Anthropology Lab

Describe structure and function of DNA and RNA.
Demonstrate how human traits are inherited.
Identify anatomical and behavioral features of non-human primates.
Compare the morphology of primates and early hominins.
Describe the biological and behavioral adaptations of the genus Homo.
Identify defining features of anatomically modern humans.

rows.title: Introduction to Archaeology

Articulate the goals, and the legal, operational, and ethical framework of cultural resource management and heritage preservation.
Demonstrate an understanding of the nature of scientific inquiry and its application in archaeological research.
Discuss the relationship between anthropology and archaeology.
Identify the various archaeological theories, methods, and techniques used to investigate the human past.
Illustrate the use of archaeological methods with reference to cultural sequences.

Define processes of culture change.
Describe archaeological and linguistic tools used to learn the migrations of early residents of the new world.
Differentiate between the various types of technology used by Paleoindians and Native North Americans.

Describe and execute techniques used to assess sex, age, stature, and ancestry of human skeletal remains.

Identify human bones and teeth and some of their features.

Evaluate the steps necessary to establish a positive identification from human skeletal remains.

rows.title: Art Appreciation

Identify, analyze, and discuss the functions of art and architecture and the roles of artists in diverse cultures.

Demonstrate conceptual thinking and implementation of concept in a variety of media.

Utilize a variety of media and techniques to creatively express self.

rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Learning Outcomes

Translate ideas and visual experience into tactile forms objects using both formal and conceptual approaches.

rows.title: Drawing  I

Create drawings that demonstrate the basic principles of spatial illusion through the application of linear, atmospheric, and other perspective systems.
Utilize a variety of lines and mark making in drawing.

Accurately describe forms and space through gradations of value.
Utilize and apply a wide range of drawing materials and techniques.
Develop expressive content through manipulation of line, form, value, and composition.

Develop and express ideas and concepts through verbal and visual means.

Experiment with color to produce a desired effect in painting.
Implement concepts from the imagination.

Manipulate color to achieve a specific outcome or effect in compositions.

rows.title: Introduction to Printmaking

Compose a printed image for production based on aesthetic principles, and formal and conceptual approaches.
Evaluate own work and work of others with correct terminology in oral and written critiques.
Examine historical and contemporary developments and approaches in printmaking.

Implement various techniques based on the medium(s) used.
Identify basic historical, contemporary, and professional developments related to figure drawing from diverse cultures.

outcomes: Learning Outcomes

Depict the human form with a growing degree of accuracy and confidence in a variety of media, including color.

Increase critical thinking skills related to the world cultural tradition of figure drawing.
Use appropriate art terminology and concepts in discussion of figurative work.

Develop greater confidence in creative expression of self and artistic risk taking.
Employ art-related vocabulary, concepts, themes , and aesthetic content relevant to human form depiction.

Problem solve a 3D project from concept to completion.
Produce projects using basic tools and forming techniques in a safe manner.

Employ appropriate vocabulary, creative thinking, problem solving, and decision making in the creation of sculptural designs

Using basic half-tone theory in production of images; manipulate, create, and edit digital images for print and for web production.

outcomes: Learning Outcomes

Compare and contrast cellular processes and interactions between prokaryotes and eukaryotes (including metabolism, reproduction, communication).
Apply the principles of classical and molecular genetics to solve problems in genetics or biotechnology.
Relate evolutionary processes to the origin and evolution of cells.
Explain how DNA replicates and transmits genetic information within organisms.
Apply the processes of scientific inquiry and experimental design to the study of biological concepts.
Acquire, read, evaluate, apply and cite scientific literature.
Practice scientific writing.

rows.title: Animal Biology, Evolution and Ecology
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Learning Outcomes
Recognize characteristics of major animal taxa.

Construct and interpret phylogenies.

Compare different patterns of animal development and life cycles of animals and non-photosynthetic, single-celled, eukaryotic taxa.
Compare and contrast anatomical and physiological features of selected animal phyla.
Illustrate and exemplify physiological functions across the animal phyla.
Identify examples of animal behavior and explain the evolutionary significance of particular behaviors.
Describe the development, evolutionary origins and modifications of representative structures.
Describe the significance of sexual reproduction.
Describe the origin of multicellularity.
Describe mechanisms of evolutionary change, including speciation.
Provide evidence for evolution.
Acquire, use, and cite scientific literature appropriately in scientific writing.
Apply scientific methodology and reasoning through active experimentation, investigations, or other activities.
Demonstrate critical thinking/scientific reasoning skills.

Provide evidence for evolution in plants and photosynthetic protistans.
Acquire, use and cite scientific literature for scientific writing.
Apply scientific methodology and reasoning through active experimentation and experiences.
Demonstrate critical thinking and scientific reasoning skills.

outcomes: Learning Outcomes

Explain the nature and purpose of generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) and International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). Identify and illustrate how the principles of internal control are used to manage and control the firm’s resources and minimize risk.

Identify and illustrate issues relating to long-term asset acquisition, use, cost allocation, and disposal.
Distinguish between capital and revenue expenditures.

Identify and illustrate issues relating to stockholders’ equity, including issuance, repurchase of capital stock, and dividends.
Explain the importance of operating, investing and financing activities reported in the Statement of Cash Flows.
Interpret company activity, profitability, liquidity and solvency through selection and application of appropriate financial analysis tools.
Identify the ethical implications inherent in financial reporting and be able to apply strategies for addressing them.
